Vendor disable ops empty the keys, so a sloppy revive (expiration without key) re-arms it. Corpus value behind the feeds while operational: ~$26M (Bucket CDP ~$15.8M + Scallop Lend ~$10.2M).
caveats: No Move fork tooling in this environment: Sui public JSON-RPC devInspect is deprecated and GraphQL exposes no simulate mutation, so Sui verification is by deployed-bytecode disassembly + on-chain event/tx forensics (the 2026-08-29 attack is itself the end-to-end proof).

Aptos indexer (api.mainnet.aptoslabs.com/v1/graphql) rate-limited (HTTP 429) during the consumer-transaction census; the per-transaction consumer census was replaced by feed-owner + feed-staleness evidence. Which consumer contracts still call aggregator::current_result was not enumerated for all integrators.
Sui GraphQL event filters key events by the package version that was latest when indexed; all 6 version IDs were scanned to recover history.
IOTA/Movement deployments not assessed (suspended per vendor post-mortem; no endpoints/tooling used here).
Consumer USD values (~$26M) are corpus figures, not re-priced in this pass; no live extraction exists so no value is realizable today.

Aptos oracle expiration values are stored in milliseconds while the framework timestamp check uses seconds; the update-path expiration check therefore effectively never expires — this does not create an unprivileged path because the signature key compare is exact.
one_liner: External unprivileged attacker can extract ~$0 live on Sui and Aptos today: the Switchboard Move bypass was real and was executed on Sui production on 2026-08-29 (3 self-registered empty-key guardians -> enable_oracle hijack), but the vendor disabled/rotated every oracle within ~5h and shipped partial patches (v5/v6) — all 48 Sui oracles are expired and the main queue is paused, while Aptos' deployed attestation compare is 64B-vs-32B and can never validate; residual CRITICAL latent on the Sui v6 attestation path if any valid oracle with an empty key is ever revived.
